analysis.one_liner: Phases out "forever chemicals" from consumer products and industrial releases over ten years.
analysis.headline: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill alone, with zero cosponsors, and the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee has taken no action since it was referred on March 19, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires companies that make or use PFAS—"forever chemicals" that never break down and have contaminated drinking water, food packaging, clothing, and household products—to report those uses publicly, then phase out every nonessential use within ten years. It bans PFAS in fast-turning consumer categories quickly: carpets, food packaging, and juvenile products within one year; cosmetics, indoor furniture, and apparel within two. It bars releases of PFAS above detectable levels, gives EPA civil and criminal enforcement power and citizens the right to sue, makes federal agencies obey the same PFAS laws as everyone else, and closes a bankruptcy loophole that has let companies shield affiliated entities from toxic-chemical damage claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to PFAS through drinking water, food packaging, clothing, cosmetics, and household goods—essentially everyone, since these chemicals are persistent, accumulate in the body, and are associated with cancer, immune and developmental harms. Communities near PFAS release sites gain immediate-notice rights and public meetings. People harmed by exposure gain easier paths to damages under state law, including limits on statutes of repose that have blocked late-discovered harm claims.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every manufacturer and user of PFAS to file annual reports covering volumes, releases at any detectable level, health-effects information, and the number of workers exposed—published for public review, which creates a nationwide public record of who uses what and where it goes [S2][S3].

Bans PFAS in consumer categories on a fast track: carpets, rugs, fabric treatments, food packaging, and juvenile products within one year; cosmetics, indoor textiles, upholstered furniture, and apparel within two years [S3].
Phases out all nonessential PFAS uses within ten years and makes it unlawful after ten years to release any PFAS above the threshold of detection into the environment [S2][S3].

Waives federal immunity so that federal agencies must comply with federal, state, and local PFAS laws, including penalties, the same as any private party—closing a gap where defense and other federal facilities are major PFAS sources [S3].

Closes a bankruptcy escape hatch: proceedings to obtain assets from non-debtor corporate affiliates are exempted from a debtor's automatic stay in claims involving persistent, bioaccumulative, toxic chemicals, making it harder for companies facing mass toxic-tort liability to wall off related entities and their assets [S2][S3].

Expands accountability through citizen suits and provisions addressing state-law damages actions, including statutes of repose that have cut off lawsuits over harms discovered years after exposure [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers that produce, import, or process PFAS and the many product makers that depend on them—apparel, carpet, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture, and industrial suppliers—face reporting fees, rapid product bans in some categories, a ten-year phaseout of nonessential uses, penalties for illegal releases, and greater liability exposure. Some compliance and litigation costs could pass through to consumer prices. Publicly owned water systems and treatment works are explicitly excluded from the definition of manufacturer or user, so ratepayers do not bear direct phaseout obligations under this bill [S3].

drawbacks.text: Reformulation costs for PFAS-using products could raise prices, and some uses have no proven alternatives—outdoor gear for severe wet conditions gets a longer, five-year phaseout precisely because a workable substitute is harder to develop [S3].

The timeline is ambitious and depends on sequencing that lags: the National Academies' scientific review can take up to three years, and essential-use designations cannot be finalized until after the first report following that review, leaving companies and regulators uncertainty about which uses survive as the ten-year deadline approaches [S3].

Compliance costs are real, including annual reports and default fees set at $100,000 if EPA fails to finalize a fee rule within two years; the bill allows reduced fees for small manufacturers but does not guarantee them [S3].

Expanded citizen suits and the provisions affecting state-law damages actions would increase litigation and settlement exposure for PFAS-related companies, some of which could surface in product prices [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is large and long-lived: PFAS do not break down, exposure is nearly universal, and cleanup costs fall heavily on water systems and taxpayers, so preventing contamination at the source is cheaper than remediating it later. The costs are genuine but bounded by design—essential uses critical for health and safety with no safer alternative can be designated and continued, small manufacturers can get reduced fees, and product bans phase in over one to five years. The bill is broad, and its complexity (a decade-long phaseout driven by petitions, National Academies reviews, and EPA rulemakings) creates implementation risk, but the core trade favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced S. 4153 on March 19, 2026; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, and that referral is the last action of any kind in the record [S5].
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor—zero, as of the latest cosponsor list [S4].
With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and chairing the committee of referral, the bill has no announced path to a hearing or floor vote in this Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, PFAS manufacturers and the consumer-product makers that depend on the chemicals continue current practices, while communities with contaminated water keep bearing the exposure and the cleanup bills. So far, the industry is better off and the public is not.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote reported in the action history.

against.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral.

against.name: PFAS-producing chemical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Have broadly opposed mandatory PFAS phaseouts and liability expansion through lobbying and litigation against EPA and state PFAS rules.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been taken, so there is no roll call to split; the only measurable support is one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, in a Senate Republicans control 55 seats to 47 for Democrats and independents.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers (chemical producers, importers, and processors)
industries.note: The bill forces a full phaseout of nonessential production and use within ten years, bans releases above detectable levels, and imposes civil and criminal penalties for violations. The industry's interest in continuing to make and sell these persistent chemicals runs against the public's interest in uncontaminated water and lower body burdens.

industries.industry: PFAS-using consumer product makers (apparel, carpet, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture)
industries.note: Fast-track sales bans hit carpets, food packaging, and juvenile products within one year and cosmetics, furniture, and apparel within two, forcing reformulation. Their continued sales of PFAS-treated goods are exactly what the public is exposed to, though some reformulation costs could appear in prices.

The bill addresses state-law damages actions and exempts claims against non-debtor affiliates from bankruptcy's automatic stay, shrinking routes companies have used to contain mass toxic-chemical liabilities. What protects those companies' balance sheets has historically meant unpaid cleanup and health costs for communities.

industries.industry: Public water systems and treatment works
industries.note: They are expressly excluded from the definitions of manufacturer and user, so they avoid direct phaseout obligations and fees, while upstream bans reduce the PFAS load reaching their plants—shifting cost burden away from ratepayers.

The bill funds Centers of Excellence for PFAS water assessment and remediation, prioritizes destruction of PFAS stocks, and requires monitoring and reporting—all of which expand demand for detection and cleanup services whose work serves the public's interest in clean water.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and referral to a Republican-chaired committee, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing, markup, or floor vote before this Congress ends; single-sponsor environmental bills at this stage routinely die in committee, as earlier PFAS phaseout proposals have.
